bridges.mechanism: Sharp escalations producing cross-border strikes, civilian casualties, or novel weapon effects prompt near-term government emergency reviews and expansion of export controls and oversight specifically targeting dual‑use AI capabilities and procurement rules.

A marked escalation in kinetic operations generates abrupt re-pricing across commodities, equity risk premia and FX (via supply shocks, sanctions and risk sentiment), increasing the speed and magnitude with which shocks transmit between asset classes.

Sustained high-intensity conventional fighting forces the U.S. to deepen alliance coordination, forward deployments, and contingency planning (and prompts reciprocal Chinese military/diplomatic responses), directly raising perceived strategic risk and bilateral security friction.

A surge in kinetic operations in Ukraine forces the US and its partners to reallocate military assets, political attention, and intelligence collection toward Europe, reducing time, presence, and operational coordination available to sustain tight alignment among regional actors confronting Iran.

Sustained high operational tempo and attrition of remotely piloted systems in the conflict forces militaries and prime contractors to field drones with higher on-board decision-making (route/target selection, collision avoidance) to maintain effectiveness, raising the average autonomy level of deployed models.

Rapid battlefield adoption and export of armed and dual‑use UAV capabilities in Ukraine triggers new U.S. export controls, stricter export licensing and allied technology screening aimed at China, increasing unpredictability of trade and tech rules between the U.S. and China.

Rapid battlefield adoption and refinement of offensive drones in Ukraine accelerates diffusion of tactics, designs, and operational doctrine to state and proxy actors in the Middle East, raising US and regional policymakers' perception of imminent, lower-threshold kinetic escalation risks vis-à-vis Iran and its proxies.

Damage or outages to energy and telecom infrastructure cause degraded inputs (latency, lost telemetry, degraded sensors) for deployed AI systems, increasing malfunction frequency and cascading safety incidents that require remediation.

Widespread strikes on energy, telecoms, or payment/clearing infrastructure in the theater disrupt trading operations, increase transaction costs and settlement risk, and prompt dealers and funds to withdraw, reducing liquidity in affected markets.

Major disruptions to European critical infrastructure that threaten energy and trade stability drive the US to open or expand diplomatic channels with Gulf states, intermediaries, and even adversaries to coordinate energy security measures and deconfliction, increasing overall diplomatic engagement intensity in the US–Iran theater.

A decline in Russian oil export flows tightens global crude and refined fuel supply, lifting energy prices and near-term inflation expectations and causing markets to price in higher central-bank policy paths.

Higher Russian oil export flows (or restoration of constrained flows) calms energy-market volatility and lowers geopolitical risk premia, improving investor risk appetite for assets exposed to U.S.–China tensions; the converse (drops in flow) depress sentiment.

A drop in Russian oil exports tightens global supply and creates demand for alternative crude, prompting the US to intensify enforcement and expand sanctions measures to prevent sanction circumvention via increased Iranian exports and third‑party facilitation.

Interruptions to semiconductor, power, and logistics supply chains increase hardware lead times and project risk, causing venture and corporate investors to delay or reduce capital allocations to AI hardware‑dependent projects and startups.

Persistent disruptions to industrial and input supply chains raise inflation persistence and expected longer-run inflation, which lifts term premia and pushes up long-duration sovereign yields as investors demand compensation for higher expected inflation.

Widespread interruption of critical inputs and routes tied to the war prompts high‑visibility bilateral and multilateral diplomatic outreach, public assurances and signaling (trade negotiations, port/route security talks) between Washington and Beijing as each seeks to protect or secure supply lines.

Highly visible public diplomatic confrontations and accusations between the US and China spur domestic legislators and regulators to open hearings and propose oversight measures targeting foreign‑linked AI capabilities, raising scrutiny intensity.

More public and antagonistic US–China diplomatic signaling prompts China to deepen energy purchases from Russia as both a supply-security move and political signal, raising the volume of Russian oil exports directed to Asian markets.

Escalatory public signaling between Washington and Beijing prompts US policymakers to increase formal and back‑channel diplomatic contacts with Iran and Gulf partners to deconflict risks to energy flows and reassure regional actors.

Rising US–China security frictions prompt accelerated military procurement and defense R&D for stand‑off and decision‑support systems, leading firms and states to deploy AI with greater on‑platform autonomy to meet contested operational requirements.

Elevated strategic security concerns drive governments to expand export controls, national security reviews, and procurement restrictions on AI technologies, producing a measurable uptick in regulatory attention and enforcement actions.

Acute rises in military/security tensions (e.g., Taiwan strait incidents or South China Sea confrontations) prompt market-makers and principal liquidity providers to pull back, widen quoted spreads and raise internal risk limits, materially reducing depth and increasing execution costs.

Rising US–China security tensions pull US/Western operational focus and some high-end assets toward the Indo‑Pacific and induce more cautious or delayed Western force-projection and materiel flows to Europe, which Russia can exploit to increase conventional operations in Ukraine.

A rise in US–China strategic tensions increases US and regional policymakers' threat perceptions and lowers tolerance for simultaneous crises, so any Iranian provocation is judged likelier to spiral into military escalation.

Sustained elevation of US–China security frictions drives temporary redeployment and prioritization of naval and air assets to the Indo‑Pacific, reducing persistent US presence and interdiction capacity around Persian Gulf chokepoints and thereby degrading chokepoint security.

A marked deterioration in investor sentiment tied to US–China rivalry triggers broad risk-off flows and forced deleveraging that synchronise selling across equities, credit, FX and commodities, increasing the speed and magnitude of cross-asset spillovers.

Escalating, unpredictable export controls and cross‑border compliance rules tied to the rivalry cause venture funds and corporate investors to delay, divert, or withhold capital from AI startups and projects exposed to bilateral trade or sanction risk.

Escalating, unpredictable trade and technology regulations (export controls, blacklists, investment bans) raise sovereign and currency risk premia and prompt foreign holders to reduce duration exposure, pushing up long-term government bond yields.

Rising US–China regulatory uncertainty (export controls, sanctions on Chinese entities) incentivizes US authorities to expand secondary sanctions and compliance enforcement targeting China‑Iran trade networks, increasing overall sanctions pressure on Iranian-linked actors.

Escalating sanctions on Iran push Tehran to deepen military-technical sales and barter with partners (notably Russia) as revenue and leverage avenues, increasing transfers of armed/UAS systems that raise drone employment in the Ukraine theater.

Broader and tighter sanctions tied to the US–Iran standoff increase banking, insurance and logistics frictions for regional trade, producing knock-on interruptions and delays in international procurement and transport links that feed into supply chains connected to the Russia–Ukraine conflict.

Heightened insecurity at maritime choke points raises demand for AI-enabled maritime ISR, autonomous vessels, and logistics-optimization tools, redirecting private and defense-related capital into AI startups and projects addressing those needs.

Deterioration of security in major maritime chokepoints raises near-term oil-price risk and expected headline inflation, prompting markets to re-price toward a higher path of central-bank policy rates.

Worsening security at Gulf/Red Sea chokepoints (attacks, closures, insurance pullback) forces rerouting, reduces tanker throughput and effective export capacity, and thereby lowers global oil export flows relevant to markets that also affect the Russia–Ukraine theater.

Heightened contestation or attacks in Middle Eastern maritime chokepoints trigger emergency trade measures, stricter routing rules and provisional export controls by the US and partners, producing immediate unpredictability in rules governing trade and strategic-technology flows between the US and China.

A spike in perceived risk of military escalation prompts legislators and security agencies to fast-track tighter AI-related export controls, procurement rules and oversight (especially for dual‑use and defense-adjacent systems), raising overall regulatory attention and intervention.

Rising fears of kinetic confrontation push militaries and contractors to prioritize and fund more autonomous sensing, targeting and navigation systems to operate in contested environments, increasing the average autonomy of deployed models.

A sudden rise in perceived probability of military escalation causes market-makers and principal liquidity providers to pull back and widen spreads, reducing depth and increasing transaction costs across fixed-income and FX markets.

A sharp rise in perceived risk of US–Iran military escalation prompts US and NATO to reassign forces and air/missile-defense assets toward the Middle East and reduces Western operational focus, creating opportunities for Russia to intensify conventional operations in Ukraine.

A rising perception of imminent US–Iran military escalation causes the US to surge naval and air deployments and readiness plans that force China to increase patrols, contingency planning and military signaling in response, directly raising bilateral security tensions.

Higher average autonomy in deployed models reduces operator workload and enables more reliable autonomous targeting, swarming, and sortie management, which militaries accelerate to increase drone operational tempo and deployment rates in the Russia–Ukraine theater.

A demonstrable rise in deployed AI autonomy narrows decision cycles and increases misperception risk, prompting defensive measures (e.g., tighter rules of engagement, deployment of countermeasures) that elevate strategic-security tensions between the two powers.

Higher deployed autonomy in naval and aerial systems enables more frequent, harder-to-interdict swarm/loitering harassment and remote attacks around the Strait of Hormuz and nearby lanes, degrading operational security of those chokepoints.

High-frequency or widely publicized AI safety incidents trigger rapid risk-off moves and concentrated selling in AI-exposed instruments, causing market-makers to widen spreads and reduce depth, thereby worsening liquidity.

A rise in AI safety incidents (misidentifications, unintended strikes, communication failures) produces immediate operational risk and loss of trust among commanders, prompting temporary grounding, stricter human-in-the-loop requirements, or reduced mission profiles for drone units.

High-profile AI safety failures—especially involving surveillance, autonomy in critical infrastructure, or military-adjacent systems—produce mutual accusations, emergency policy responses, and force-posturing that raise perceived military and strategic risk between the US and China.

A spike in AI safety incidents (e.g., autonomous systems misfiring, misattributed cyber operations or false alarms) increases uncertainty and attribution risk between Washington and Tehran, making policymakers and publics judge a military escalation as more likely.

Heightened regulatory scrutiny that raises compliance costs and slows deployment of productivity-enhancing AI dampens growth and inflation outlooks, leading markets to price a lower expected path for short-term policy rates.

Intensified AI-related regulatory scrutiny in major supplier states spurs export controls, licensing bottlenecks, and tighter vetting of compute/hardware transfers, directly delaying deliveries of components and software used in military and commercial supply chains affecting the conflict zone.

A sudden increase in legislative and oversight actions on AI (export controls, licensing, approvals) directly raises unpredictability about cross-border rules and compliance burdens for US–China technology exchanges, increasing regulatory uncertainty for actors in the bilateral relationship.

A sudden increase in capital directed into AI equity and infrastructure raises corporate issuance and risk-on positioning while diverting demand from long-duration sovereign paper, mechanically pushing up long-term government yields.

Rising investment into AI by the U.S. and its partners accelerates joint procurement, interoperability projects and intelligence-sharing architectures, which strengthens alignment and operational coordination among regional coalitions confronting Iran.

Intense media coverage of AI breakthroughs or failures synchronizes retail and algorithmic sentiment across markets, amplifying correlation and accelerating the transmission of shocks between equities, bonds, FX and commodities.

Surges in media coverage and public debate about AI incidents and risks force both capitals to engage in visible public diplomacy (statements, joint or competing initiatives, summits) to reassure domestic audiences and signal positions to the other side.

Higher long‑term sovereign yields raise the discount rate used to value growth companies and infrastructure, compressing valuations and reducing equity and private investment flows into AI firms and projects that rely on long‑dated returns.

Rising long‑term sovereign yields raise corporate borrowing and trade‑finance costs, forcing firms to reduce inventory financing and delay or cancel shipments, producing measurable interruptions and slowdowns in cross‑border supply chains serving the theater.

Rising global long-term sovereign yields increase discount rates and funding costs, triggering portfolio rebalancing away from higher-risk, US–China–exposed assets and thereby reducing aggregate investor risk appetite toward bilateral-exposed instruments.

Rising expected short-term policy rates increase borrowing costs and investors' discount rates, directly lowering venture allocations and corporate capex for long‑horizon AI projects by making them less attractive relative to safer/higher‑yield alternatives.

Higher expected policy rates raise borrowing costs and fiscal strain for Western governments, increasing political pressure to curb costly external military assistance and procurement for Ukraine and thereby reducing the tempo and scale of Ukrainian operations.

Improved market liquidity reduces trade‑finance and commodity‑hedging costs and makes it easier to roll financing for tankers and traders, increasing the likelihood that crude and product cargoes are shipped on schedule and raising realized export flows.

Sharp deterioration in market liquidity produces large, disorderly price moves in cross-border positions and prompts authorities to introduce emergency trading rules, reporting requirements or capital-flow measures directed at foreign/strategic investments, increasing regulatory unpredictability in the US–China policy space.

A sharp deterioration in market liquidity increases the likelihood that any military flare-up will trigger outsized asset-price dislocations and funding stress, which incentivizes US policymakers and regional actors to avoid kinetic actions and therefore lowers near-term perceptions of imminent escalation.

When shocks rapidly transmit from bonds to equities and tech sectors, visible linkages between AI companies and systemic market stress prompt policymakers and watchdogs to initiate inquiries and tighten oversight of AI practices and market conduct.

When shocks in one asset class rapidly transmit to equities, FX and credit across US–China exposures, governments and central banks escalate visible public communications and gestures (statements, coordinated releases, reputational assignment) to calm markets and influence counterpart behavior, raising diplomatic signaling intensity.

Stronger and faster cross-asset spillovers transmit shocks from oil and insurance markets into shipping costs and insurer capacity, raising transit risk and observable contestation around maritime chokepoints and thereby degrading chokepoint security.

Kinetic Conflict Intensity
nodes.description: Measures the overall intensity and scale of conventional and proxy military operations across the theater, including ground, air, and naval engagements.

nodes.label: Hybrid Attack Rate
nodes.description: Measures the rate at which hybrid operations (sabotage, cyber intrusions, irregular raids, and non-conventional strikes) occur over time.

nodes.label: Drone Use Intensity
nodes.description: Measures the prevalence, operational tempo, and lethality of unmanned aerial systems employed in offensive and support roles.

nodes.label: Critical Infrastructure Disruption
nodes.description: Measures the aggregate functional disruption to critical infrastructure sectors (energy, telecoms, transport, industrial) at a given time.

nodes.label: Oil Export Flow
nodes.description: Measures the volumetric flow rate of crude oil and refined product exports moving through global trade routes and terminals.

nodes.label: Oil Price Level
nodes.description: Measures the prevailing market price level for benchmark crude oil and major refined products.

nodes.label: Emergency Oil Reserves
nodes.description: Measures the aggregated stock level of emergency or strategic petroleum reserves available for release to markets.

nodes.label: Supply Chain Disruption
nodes.description: Measures the degree of interruption to logistics, manufacturing inputs, and cross-border supply chain continuity.

nodes.label: Defense Deployment Level
nodes.description: Measures the scale and concentration of deployed defensive assets and countermeasures (air defenses, patrols, escorts, cybersecurity) in contested areas.

nodes.label: Sanctions and Trade Restriction Intensity
nodes.description: Measures the breadth and severity of economic restrictions, asset controls, and trade barriers imposed across actors and sectors.

nodes.label: Corporate Withdrawal Rate
nodes.description: Measures the rate at which firms reduce exposure through divestments, production cuts, asset freezes, or relocation decisions.

nodes.label: Market Volatility Level
nodes.description: Measures short-term volatility and uncertainty in financial and commodity markets tied to geopolitical and supply shocks.

nodes.label: Geopolitical Risk Perception
nodes.description: Measures collective perceptions and expectations of political and security risk among market actors, policymakers, and publics.

nodes.label: Energy Supply Resilience
nodes.description: Measures the capacity of energy systems to absorb, redistribute, and recover from disruptions to production and transport.

nodes.label: Chokepoint Vulnerability
nodes.description: Measures the exposure and susceptibility of key maritime and transit chokepoints to interdiction, closure, or disruption.

nodes.label: Defense Technology Adoption Rate
nodes.description: Measures the pace at which countermeasures (counter-drone systems, hardened infrastructure, monitoring tech) are deployed and integrated.

Diplomatic signaling intensity
nodes.description: The continuous intensity and visibility of public diplomatic gestures, pageantry and official signaling between negotiating actors.

nodes.label: Trade barrier level
nodes.description: The average effective height of tariff and non-tariff barriers constraining cross-border goods and services flows.

nodes.label: Low-tariff agreement scope
nodes.description: The breadth and share of goods and services covered by preferential or reduced-tariff arrangements between parties.

nodes.label: AI cooperation depth
nodes.description: The substantive depth and institutionalization of cooperative channels, information exchange and joint measures in artificial intelligence.

nodes.label: Security tension level
nodes.description: The prevailing intensity of strategic-security frictions and perceived military risk across contested regional issues.

nodes.label: Technological competition intensity
nodes.description: The degree of competitive pressure in key technology domains, including R&D rivalry, export controls and strategic decoupling incentives.

nodes.label: Supply-chain fragmentation
nodes.description: The extent to which production networks are geographically dispersed, re-shored or segmented across alternative supplier blocs.

nodes.label: Investor sentiment
nodes.description: The aggregate market perception and risk appetite of investors toward assets exposed to bilateral political and economic dynamics.

nodes.label: Capital flow rate
nodes.description: The volume per unit time of cross-border financial inflows and outflows into assets and sectors linked to the bilateral relationship.

nodes.label: Market volatility
nodes.description: The realized short- to medium-term variability of asset prices and exchange rates influenced by geopolitical-economic shocks.

nodes.label: Corporate restructuring rate
nodes.description: The rate at which firms alter investment, supply-chain design, joint ventures and market strategies in response to strategic pressures.

nodes.label: Allied trust level
nodes.description: The aggregate level of confidence and policy alignment among third-party partners and alliances regarding bilateral commitments.

nodes.label: Domestic political legitimacy
nodes.description: The perceived domestic approval and institutional legitimacy of national leadership as influenced by foreign-policy engagements.

nodes.label: Regulatory uncertainty
nodes.description: The prevailing unpredictability and clarity of policy and regulatory rules affecting trade, investment and strategic technologies.

nodes.label: Media spectacle intensity
nodes.description: The magnitude and salience of public media coverage and symbolic framing of events and interactions.

nodes.label: Policy coordination capacity
nodes.description: The institutional ability and bandwidth to design, negotiate and implement sustained cross-jurisdictional policy measures.

Military readiness level
nodes.description: Measures aggregate operational readiness and mobilization posture of armed forces directly involved in the confrontation.

nodes.label: Diplomatic engagement intensity
nodes.description: Measures frequency, scale and intensity of formal and informal diplomatic contacts and negotiations among parties and intermediaries.

nodes.label: Sanctions pressure level
nodes.description: Measures cumulative severity and scope of economic punitive measures applied against an actor in the dispute.

nodes.label: Nuclear program militarization
nodes.description: Measures the degree to which a nuclear program is oriented toward weapons development and military use rather than civilian purposes.

nodes.label: Chokepoint security
nodes.description: Measures the operational security and contested control of critical maritime transit chokepoints and sea lanes.

nodes.label: Mediation activity rate
nodes.description: Measures the rate and intensity of third-party mediation initiatives, shuttle diplomacy, and facilitated talks.

nodes.label: Regional coalition cohesion
nodes.description: Measures the alignment, coordination and mutual support among regional actors and informal coalitions relevant to the confrontation.

nodes.label: Escalation risk perception
nodes.description: Measures policymaker and public perception of the probability and imminence of military escalation in the conflict.

nodes.label: Strike frequency
nodes.description: Measures the rate of kinetic military strikes and offensive actions in the operational theater.

nodes.label: Deterrence credibility
nodes.description: Measures perceived credibility and effectiveness of deterrent threats and retaliatory assurances among adversaries.

nodes.label: Sanctions evasion capacity
nodes.description: Measures the systemic ability to bypass, circumvent, or mitigate the effects of economic and financial sanctions.

nodes.label: Information disruption level
nodes.description: Measures the intensity of information operations, propaganda, communications interference and signal-shaping efforts.

nodes.label: Economic isolation degree
nodes.description: Measures the extent of trade, financial and transport isolation imposed on an actor within the confrontation.

nodes.label: Energy disruption risk
nodes.description: Measures the probability and expected severity of interruptions to energy exports, transit, and global supply linked to the dispute.

nodes.label: Negotiation flexibility
nodes.description: Measures the willingness of parties to make concessions, adjust demands, and adopt creative compromises in talks.

nodes.label: Mediator influence level
nodes.description: Measures the practical influence and leverage of intermediaries and mediation channels in shaping outcomes.

Domestic push toward Iran nuclear weaponization
AI boom collides with safety, regulation, and market pressures
AI research & innovation pace
nodes.description: The instantaneous rate at which new capabilities, architectures, and algorithmic advances are produced and integrated into models and systems.

nodes.label: Average model autonomy
nodes.description: The typical degree of agentic ability and independent decision-making exhibited by deployed AI systems across the ecosystem.

nodes.label: AI safety incident frequency
nodes.description: The rate at which AI systems cause harms, misbehave, or trigger safety-related failures requiring remediation or public response.

nodes.label: AI-related data leakage frequency
nodes.description: The rate of unauthorized disclosures, exfiltrations, or unintended exposures of data attributable to AI development or deployment activities.

nodes.label: Regulatory scrutiny intensity
nodes.description: The prevailing level of legislative, oversight, and policy attention aimed at constraining or governing AI activities and products.

nodes.label: Regulatory and legal enforcement rate
nodes.description: The frequency and severity of legal actions, fines, injunctions, or other enforcement measures applied to AI actors and deployments.

nodes.label: Capital flow into AI
nodes.description: The net rate of financial investment (equity, debt, venture funding, and corporate spend) directed into AI research, startups, and infrastructure.

nodes.label: Aggregate AI valuation level
nodes.description: The market aggregate valuation or capital market pricing attributable to AI-exposed companies, assets, and projects.

nodes.label: Available compute capacity
nodes.description: The total available high-performance compute resources (training and inference capacity) accessible to AI development and deployment.

nodes.label: Hardware supply-chain risk
nodes.description: The degree of disruption risk, lead-time variability, and scarcity in the hardware and component supply chains that support AI infrastructure.

nodes.label: Cost of capital for AI projects
nodes.description: The prevailing effective financing cost (interest rates, required returns, discount rates) faced by firms and projects investing in AI.

nodes.label: Qualified AI talent supply
nodes.description: The stock of individuals with the skills and experience available for AI research, engineering, and deployment roles.

nodes.label: AI talent mobility rate
nodes.description: The rate at which qualified AI personnel move between employers, sectors, geographies, or exit the field entirely.

nodes.label: Public trust and confidence
nodes.description: The aggregate level of societal trust in AI systems' safety, reliability, and benefit to individuals and communities.

nodes.label: Media and public attention to AI
nodes.description: The volume and intensity of media coverage and public discourse focused on AI incidents, capabilities, and controversies.

nodes.label: Corporate transparency & openness
nodes.description: The degree to which organizations share model details, safety practices, data provenance, and third‑party auditability about their AI systems.

Long-term sovereign yields
nodes.description: The prevailing levels of yields on long-duration government bonds across major maturities.

nodes.label: Yield-curve slope
nodes.description: The difference between long-term and short-term sovereign yields, capturing term structure shape and steepness.

nodes.label: Policy-rate expectations
nodes.description: Market-implied expected path of short-term policy rates over the forecast horizon.

nodes.label: Central-bank signaling intensity
nodes.description: The frequency, clarity and strength of central-bank communications and forward guidance that influence market interpretation of policy stance.

nodes.label: Macro data surprise flow
nodes.description: The stream and magnitude of incoming macroeconomic releases relative to consensus expectations (positive or negative surprises).

nodes.label: Inflation trend
nodes.description: The underlying trajectory and persistence of consumer price inflation over time.

nodes.label: Economic growth momentum
nodes.description: The recent rate of change and acceleration of real economic activity or output growth.

nodes.label: Oil price level
nodes.description: The prevailing market price of crude oil as a representative commodity-price indicator.

nodes.label: Market liquidity conditions
nodes.description: The ease and cost of executing sizable trades in financial markets without inducing large price moves.

nodes.label: Risk premia in risky assets
nodes.description: The additional expected return investors demand for holding risky assets instead of safe assets.

nodes.label: Safe-asset demand flow
nodes.description: Net flows and shifts in investor demand into recognized safe-haven assets over time.

nodes.label: Cross-asset spillover intensity
nodes.description: The strength and speed with which shocks in one asset class transmit to prices and volatility in other asset classes.

nodes.label: Implied volatility
nodes.description: Market-implied expected near-term price volatility derived from option prices across asset classes.

nodes.label: Credit spread levels
nodes.description: Average yield premium of corporate or non-sovereign debt over comparable sovereign yields reflecting credit risk compensation.

nodes.label: Foreign-exchange pressure
nodes.description: Directional stress, volatility and capital-flow-driven pressure experienced in currency markets.

nodes.label: Geopolitical risk tension
nodes.description: The intensity and perceived probability of geopolitical developments that could materially disrupt markets and trades.

Rising fears of kinetic confrontation push militaries and contractors to prioritize and fund more autonomous sensing, targeting and navigation systems to operate in contested environments, increasing the average autonomy of deployed models.

A sudden rise in perceived probability of military escalation causes market-makers and principal liquidity providers to pull back and widen spreads, reducing depth and increasing transaction costs across fixed-income and FX markets.

A sharp rise in perceived risk of US–Iran military escalation prompts US and NATO to reassign forces and air/missile-defense assets toward the Middle East and reduces Western operational focus, creating opportunities for Russia to intensify conventional operations in Ukraine.

A rising perception of imminent US–Iran military escalation causes the US to surge naval and air deployments and readiness plans that force China to increase patrols, contingency planning and military signaling in response, directly raising bilateral security tensions.

Higher average autonomy in deployed models reduces operator workload and enables more reliable autonomous targeting, swarming, and sortie management, which militaries accelerate to increase drone operational tempo and deployment rates in the Russia–Ukraine theater.

A demonstrable rise in deployed AI autonomy narrows decision cycles and increases misperception risk, prompting defensive measures (e.g., tighter rules of engagement, deployment of countermeasures) that elevate strategic-security tensions between the two powers.

Higher deployed autonomy in naval and aerial systems enables more frequent, harder-to-interdict swarm/loitering harassment and remote attacks around the Strait of Hormuz and nearby lanes, degrading operational security of those chokepoints.

High-frequency or widely publicized AI safety incidents trigger rapid risk-off moves and concentrated selling in AI-exposed instruments, causing market-makers to widen spreads and reduce depth, thereby worsening liquidity.

A rise in AI safety incidents (misidentifications, unintended strikes, communication failures) produces immediate operational risk and loss of trust among commanders, prompting temporary grounding, stricter human-in-the-loop requirements, or reduced mission profiles for drone units.

High-profile AI safety failures—especially involving surveillance, autonomy in critical infrastructure, or military-adjacent systems—produce mutual accusations, emergency policy responses, and force-posturing that raise perceived military and strategic risk between the US and China.

A spike in AI safety incidents (e.g., autonomous systems misfiring, misattributed cyber operations or false alarms) increases uncertainty and attribution risk between Washington and Tehran, making policymakers and publics judge a military escalation as more likely.

Heightened regulatory scrutiny that raises compliance costs and slows deployment of productivity-enhancing AI dampens growth and inflation outlooks, leading markets to price a lower expected path for short-term policy rates.

Intensified AI-related regulatory scrutiny in major supplier states spurs export controls, licensing bottlenecks, and tighter vetting of compute/hardware transfers, directly delaying deliveries of components and software used in military and commercial supply chains affecting the conflict zone.

A sudden increase in legislative and oversight actions on AI (export controls, licensing, approvals) directly raises unpredictability about cross-border rules and compliance burdens for US–China technology exchanges, increasing regulatory uncertainty for actors in the bilateral relationship.

A sudden increase in capital directed into AI equity and infrastructure raises corporate issuance and risk-on positioning while diverting demand from long-duration sovereign paper, mechanically pushing up long-term government yields.

Rising investment into AI by the U.S. and its partners accelerates joint procurement, interoperability projects and intelligence-sharing architectures, which strengthens alignment and operational coordination among regional coalitions confronting Iran.

Intense media coverage of AI breakthroughs or failures synchronizes retail and algorithmic sentiment across markets, amplifying correlation and accelerating the transmission of shocks between equities, bonds, FX and commodities.

Surges in media coverage and public debate about AI incidents and risks force both capitals to engage in visible public diplomacy (statements, joint or competing initiatives, summits) to reassure domestic audiences and signal positions to the other side.

Higher long‑term sovereign yields raise the discount rate used to value growth companies and infrastructure, compressing valuations and reducing equity and private investment flows into AI firms and projects that rely on long‑dated returns.

Rising long‑term sovereign yields raise corporate borrowing and trade‑finance costs, forcing firms to reduce inventory financing and delay or cancel shipments, producing measurable interruptions and slowdowns in cross‑border supply chains serving the theater.

Rising global long-term sovereign yields increase discount rates and funding costs, triggering portfolio rebalancing away from higher-risk, US–China–exposed assets and thereby reducing aggregate investor risk appetite toward bilateral-exposed instruments.

Rising expected short-term policy rates increase borrowing costs and investors' discount rates, directly lowering venture allocations and corporate capex for long‑horizon AI projects by making them less attractive relative to safer/higher‑yield alternatives.

Higher expected policy rates raise borrowing costs and fiscal strain for Western governments, increasing political pressure to curb costly external military assistance and procurement for Ukraine and thereby reducing the tempo and scale of Ukrainian operations.

Improved market liquidity reduces trade‑finance and commodity‑hedging costs and makes it easier to roll financing for tankers and traders, increasing the likelihood that crude and product cargoes are shipped on schedule and raising realized export flows.

Sharp deterioration in market liquidity produces large, disorderly price moves in cross-border positions and prompts authorities to introduce emergency trading rules, reporting requirements or capital-flow measures directed at foreign/strategic investments, increasing regulatory unpredictability in the US–China policy space.

A sharp deterioration in market liquidity increases the likelihood that any military flare-up will trigger outsized asset-price dislocations and funding stress, which incentivizes US policymakers and regional actors to avoid kinetic actions and therefore lowers near-term perceptions of imminent escalation.

When shocks rapidly transmit from bonds to equities and tech sectors, visible linkages between AI companies and systemic market stress prompt policymakers and watchdogs to initiate inquiries and tighten oversight of AI practices and market conduct.

When shocks in one asset class rapidly transmit to equities, FX and credit across US–China exposures, governments and central banks escalate visible public communications and gestures (statements, coordinated releases, reputational assignment) to calm markets and influence counterpart behavior, raising diplomatic signaling intensity.

Stronger and faster cross-asset spillovers transmit shocks from oil and insurance markets into shipping costs and insurer capacity, raising transit risk and observable contestation around maritime chokepoints and thereby degrading chokepoint security.
